title: HTTP & REST
summary: The request/response model, the methods and status codes that matter, what makes an API RESTful, and how a Java backend maps all of it to resource endpoints.
note:
1. HTTP is request→response over a stateless connection
2. Methods: GET read, POST create, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE remove
3. Status families: 2xx ok, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error
4. REST = resources as URLs, verbs as methods, stateless, representation in JSON
✎ In my words: ______________________________________________

recall.q: Which HTTP method is idempotent but not safe?
recall.a: PUT and DELETE — repeating them leaves the same end state, but they do change server state (so they are not 'safe' like GET).

recall.q: What does statelessness mean for REST?
recall.a: Each request carries everything the server needs; the server keeps no per-client session in memory between requests.

recall.q: Status code for 'authenticated but not allowed'?

shot.title: Status code families
shot.body:
| family | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| 2xx | success | 200 OK, 201 Created |
| 3xx | redirection | 301, 304 Not Modified |
| 4xx | client error | 400, 401, 403, 404 |
| 5xx | server error | 500, 502, 503 |

sections.title: The request/response model
sections.body: ✍️ HTTP is a **stateless** protocol: the client sends a request (method + URL + headers + optional body), the server returns a response (status line + headers + body). Nothing is remembered between requests unless you add cookies, tokens, or a session store. This is why REST APIs scale horizontally — any server can handle any request.

sections.title: Methods & idempotency
sections.body: ✍️ **GET** reads (safe, idempotent, cacheable). **POST** creates or triggers (not idempotent). **PUT** replaces a resource (idempotent). **PATCH** partially updates. **DELETE** removes (idempotent). Idempotent = repeating the call leaves the same end state, which matters for safe client retries.

sections.title: What makes it REST
sections.body:
✍️ REST models the domain as **resources** addressed by URLs (`/users/42`), acted on by HTTP verbs, exchanged as representations (usually JSON). Rules: stateless, uniform interface, nouns in paths not verbs (`POST /orders`, not `/createOrder`), and correct status codes.
- Good: `GET /users/42/orders`. Bad: `GET /getOrdersForUser?id=42`.
